sentences.text:
Accused JUDGMENT:
1.
The present is a complaint filed under section 16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 (PFA Act), alleging that the accused has violated the provisions of the PFA Act and Rules.

The accused Pramod Kumar Jain is stated to be the vendor-cum-proprietor of M/s. Shahi Bhog, from where the food article, that is, 'Khoya Burfi' was lifted for sampling.
2.

As per the complaint, on 10.11.2004, the food officials consisting of Food Inspector (FI) Ranjeet Singh and Field Assistant (FA) Mittra Pal under the supervision of Local Health Authority (LHA)/SDM Sh. C. P. Sharma reached along with their staff at the premises of M/s. Shahi Bhog, at F-3/5, Krishna Nagar, Delhi-51, where the accused was found conducting the business of various food articles, which were lying stored/exposed for sale for human consumption.
The FI disclosed his identity and expressed his intention to purchase a sample of Khoya Burfi from the vendor, to which he had agreed.
The sample was then lifted as per procedure prescribed under the PFA Act and Rules.
Each sample was separately packed, fastened, marked and sealed and necessary documents were prepared at the spot, including the notice as per Form-VI, panchnama, etc.
The price of sample was paid to the vendor.
Thereafter, one counterpart of the sample was sent to the Public Analyst (PA) in intact condition and the other two counterparts were deposited with SDM/LHA.

Vide report dated Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs Pramod Kumar Jain on 19 September, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/80700135/
1 02.12.2004, the PA found the sample to be adulterated on the ground that it contained added vegetable oil which was not declared as an ingredient.

sentences.text: Upon receipt of report, the SDM/LHA ordered investigation which was carried out by FI.
After completion of investigation, sanction under section 20 of the PFA Act was obtained from the Director PFA.
The complaint was then filed in the court on 02.03.2005 alleging violation of section 2(ia)(a) and (b) of PFA Act as punishable section 7/16(1)(a) of PFA Act.
3. As the complaint was filed in writing by a public servant, recording of pre-summoning evidence was dispensed with and the accused was summoned vide order dated 02.03.2005.

The accused appeared and filed an application under section 13(2) of PFA Act on 10.04.2007 thereby exercising his right to get the second counterpart of the sample analysed from Central Food Laboratory (CFL).
However, vide order dated 13.04.2007, the said application was dismissed being not maintainable as the delay could not be condoned.

Thereafter, notice of accusation under section 251 CrPC was framed against him on 14.07.2008 for commission of the offence punishable under section 7/16(1)(a) PFA Act, being violation of section 2(ia)(a) and (b) of PFA Act, to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed trial.
4. At the trial, prosecution examined three witnesses in support of its case.

PW-1 was the LHA/SDM,
PW-2 was the FI and PW-3 was the FA who were part of the team that had visited the spot for sample proceedings.

All these witnesses deposed about the proceedings conducted by them on 10.11.2004 and narrated the steps undertaken by them during the sample proceedings, including disclosing their identity, expressing intention to purchase sample for analysis, lifting the sample of 1500 gms of Khoya Burfi, cutting the same into smallest possible pieces using a clean and dry knife,
mixing/homogenizing it using a clean and dry spoon, dividing it in three parts and putting in clean and dry bottles, adding formalin (40 drops each) as preservative, fastening, sealing, marking the sample bottles, and obtaining signatures of vendor and witnesses.

They also proved the necessary documents including the vendor's receipt Ex. PW-1/A and issuance of cash memo Ex. PW-1/A1,
Notice in Form-VI Ex. PW-1/B and Panchnama Ex. PW-1/C.
One sample was deposited with PA vide PA Receipt Ex. PW-1/E and two counterparts with LHA vide receipt Ex. PW-1/D.

PA report Ex.
PW-1/F was received upon which investigation was carried out by PW-2.
Letter Ex. PW-2/A was written to accused which was not replied and letter Ex. PW-2/B was written to STO which was replied.
After completion of investigation, sanction Ex. PW-1/G was taken from the Director PFA and the complaint Ex. PW-1/H was filed in the court.

A copy of PA report with intimation letter Ex.
PW-1/I was sent to the accused through registered post vide receipt Ex. PW-1/J.
These witnesses were duly cross-examined by Ld. Defence Counsel wherein they denied that the sampling method was not proper or that the spoon / bottles used in the proceedings were not clean and dry.
5. Statement of the accused under section 313 CrPC was recorded on 04.05.2012 wherein he denied the allegations and pleaded innocence.
Though he admitted the proceedings dated 10.11.2004, yet he claimed that no efforts were made to join public witnesses and that the bottles used were not clean and dry.
He took stand that he had added badam and pista in the article which contains vegetable oil.
He stated that vanaspati was not added as an ingredient but his worker had pasted some vegetable oil in the tray to avoid sticking of burfi with the tray.
He chose to lead evidence in defence.

sentences.text:
The accused summoned record of a letter no. P-150 16/3/83- PH(F&N) PFA dated 17.10.1984,
and proved it though DW-1.
7.
The accused also examined Sh. S. N. Mahendru, a food chemical expert as DW-1 (sic: DW-1A).
He deposed that glycerine and vegetable oil are allowed as Good Manufacturing Practices so that the material does not stick to the container.
He further stated that almond seeds and pista have oil content in them.

During cross-examination, he stated that almond oil, pista oil and other vegetable oils have different chemical compositions which can be identified and that the analyst is required to identify which other oil is present in the article.

8. It is in these circumstances, Ld. SPP for the complainant has argued that the complainant has been able to establish its case against the accused beyond reasonable doubt, on the ground that the accused has not been able to rebut the findings in the PA report dated 02.12.2004.
It is submitted that all the witnesses have supported its case and no major contradiction can be seen in their testimony.

9. On the other hand, Ld. Defence Counsel has submitted that the sample proceedings were not conducted properly and that there are various contradictions and missing links in the testimony of witnesses.
Ld. Counsel has contended that the sample of burfi contained almonds and pista which were declared as ingredients and they have their own inherent oil.
It is submitted that vegetable oil is permitted to be used as a lubricant and that the accused had used oil on the tray so that the food article does not stick to the tray.
It is then argued that as per Rule 43(5) of PFA Rules, a seller of sweets is not required to declare the ingredients and thus, there is no violation of rules.
It is also argued that the complaint was filed after three months of lifting the sample which caused prejudice to the accused as he could not exercise his right under section 13(2) PFA Act on time.
10. I have heard the arguments advanced by Ld. SPP for the complainant and Ld. Defence Counsel for the accused and have carefully perused the material available on record.
11. It is to be understood that the notice framed against the accused is for violation of section 2(ia)(a) and (b) of the PFA Act.
He is not facing trial for violation of section 2(ia)(m) of PFA Act.
This is important to note because the ingredients of these offences are different and distinct.

12. Under section 2(ia)(a) of PFA Act, the prosecution has to establish that the purchaser had demanded a food article of a specific nature, substance or quality and the article sold was, to his prejudice, either not of the nature, substance or quality demanded, or was not of the nature,
substance or quality which it purported or represented to be.

Under section 2(ia)(b) of PFA Act, it has to be established that the food article contained any substance affecting injuriously the nature,
substance or quality thereof.

On the other hand, section 2(ia)(m) of PFA Act deals with situation where the quality or purity of an article falls below the prescribed standard or its constituents are present in quantities not within the prescribed limits of variability.
13. To begin with, it is an admitted position that the food article Khoya Burfi does not fall under any item of Appendix-B of the PFA Rules.

No standards have been prescribed under the Rules with Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs Pramod Kumar Jain on 19 September, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/80700135/
3 respect to 'Khoya Burfi' as a standardised food article.

entities.text: Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs Pramod Kumar Jain

sentences.text: It was thus analysed as a proprietary food.
Proprietary Food, as per Rule 37-A of PFA Rules means a food which has not been standardised under the said Rules.
Under Rule 37- A(e), proprietary food products shall not contain food additives except as provided under the rules for that food or category of food.
14. The accused has not questioned the fact that the business concern M/s. Shahi Bhog is a proprietorship concern, of which he is the proprietor.
It is not his case that he is not the proprietor of the said premises or that some other person is its proprietor.
It is again not disputed that a sample of Khoya Burfi was lifted by the food officials on 10.11.2004 from the said premises and the accused was the vendor who had sold the said article.
It is not his stand that the food article was not for sale or that it was for any purpose other than sale for human consumption.
There is no dispute about the sample having been sent to the PA on the specified date.

There is no dispute that the complaint was filed as per the procedure after obtaining sanction / consent of the Director, PFA.
15.
At this stage, it is noted that the case of the prosecution is based on the PA report dated 02.12.2004.
The sample was never sent to the CFL for analysis.
As already stated, the accused had moved an application to exercise his right under section 13(2) PFA Act but the same stood dismissed on account of delay.

Though the accused never challenged the said order which thus attained finality, yet he is still raising a defence that his right unbde3r section 13(2) PFA Act stood frustrated because the PA report with intimation letter were never served upon him.

16. As per the scheme of the Act, under section 13(2) of the Act, after institution of prosecution against the accused, the LHA is required to forward a copy of the PA report to the accused,
informing that he may apply to the Court, within 10 days of receipt of report, for getting the sample (second counterpart) analysed by CFL.
Thus, this provision mandates sending of PA report to the accused by the LHA.
It is a settled law that if the report is not so sent, it would cause prejudice to the accused and his right cannot be frustrated by the prosecution.
17. At the outset, there is no merit in the contention that the PA report was not received by the accused.
PW-1 and PW-2 both deposed about sending the copy of PA report with intimation letter Ex. PW-1/I through registered post vide receipt Ex. PW-1/J.
The postal receipt had been proved during evidence of PW-2 when office file was seen and returned.
Apparently, no objection was raised by the defence with respect to correctness of such postal receipt at the time of evidence.
Such evidence has not been rebutted by the defence anywhere.

Not even a single suggestion was given to these witnesses that the postal receipt Ex. PW-1/J was a forged or fabricated document or that no such letter was sent or that it was sent at an incorrect address.
If he was genuinely disputing the existence or correctness of the postal receipt, he should have asked the witnesses about it or have insisted on the original document to be retained on record.
But no such attempt was made.

Thus,
accused cannot take benefit on this count when no such stand was taken by him during the evidence so as to enable the witnesses to deny and rebut any such suggestion.
The accused has never denied during the evidence of the witnesses that no such letter was 'sent' to him, though he gave suggestion to PW-2 that it was not 'received' by him.
It is thus clear that letter had been sent to the accused through registered post, as deposed by witnesses on oath.

Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs Pramod Kumar Jain on 19 September, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/80700135/
4 18.

sentences.text: Once this fact is so established, section 27 of the General Clauses Act would come into play.
When a letter is sent through registered post at a correct and proper address, there would be a presumption of service under section 27 of the General Clauses Act in favour of the complainant.

The burden would not upon be the complainant to show delivery of the letter and such burden would now shift upon the accused to show that the letter was not so delivered despite having been sent at a correct address through registered post.
But the accused has not led any evidence to this effect.
No attempt was made by him to summon the records of postal department to show as to whom the letter was delivered or if it remained undelivered.
There is no evidence to show that the letter was not received by the accused, as suggested by him to the PW-2 during his cross- examination.
Accused has not shown where was he residing or was running his shop if not at this address.
19 . It is also noted that the accused has never even denied the factum of receipt of intimation letter in his statement under section 313 CrPC.
When this incriminating evidence was put to him, he simply stated that it was "a matter of record".
Visibly, he never claimed that no such letter was sent to him or received by him.
He never stated that the postal receipt was a false or forged document.
In this backdrop, there is nothing to show that the letter could not have been served upon the accused at the relevant time.
It is not his claim that he was not available at the said address or had shifted from that address.
Thus, accused has failed to rebut the presumption under section 27 of the General Clauses Act.
As PW-1 and PW-2 deposed that the registered letter was sent through registered post, the burden would be upon the accused to prove anything to the contrary.
By not leading any evidence to support his stand, the version of the accused remains unsubstantiated.
Therefore, it has to be held that the intimation letter and PA report were delivered upon the accused in due course.

The accused cannot therefore opt to simply deny the things and claim that PA report /
intimation letter was not received by him.
Thus, it is clear that the court would not assume that the right of the accused stood frustrated just like that.
Rather he had filed an application under section 13(2) PFA Act which was dismissed as mentioned above but he chose not to challenge that order before a competent authority.
20. Thus, the accused cannot contend that his right under section 13(2) of the Act stood frustrated.
It is also not a case where the right of the accused got frustrated due to any delay in filing the prosecution.

Irrespective of time taken in investigating the matter and filing the complaint after obtaining sanction, it can be noted that no amount of delay could have produced vegetable oil in the food product if it was otherwise absent.
This is particularly when the accused has not actually denied presence of vegetable oil in the article, but has only sought to justify or explain its presence.

Therefore, section 13(2) of PFA Act would not come to rescue of the accused from any angle.
21.

With such material in hand, it is clear that the food article "Pista Burfi" is not a standardised food article and thus, no standards have been prescribed under the PFA Rules which can be said to have been violated.
Since no standards have been prescribed for this commodity, it would be clear that section 2(ia)(m) of the PFA Act would not apply.
Such provision would be applicable only where the quality or purity of a food article falls below the prescribed standards.

But when there are no standards prescribed, there can be no violation under section 2(ia)(m) and precisely for this reason,
no prosecution is continuing under this provision.

But to say, that since there are no standards for Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs Pramod Kumar Jain on 19 September, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/80700135/
5

entities.text: Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs Pramod Kumar Jain
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: this food article and thus there can be no adulteration, would certainly be not correct.
Even if a food article is not a standardised food article, it has to be free from adulteration and has to be pass the other tests upon being considered as a proprietary food.

It cannot be said that since there are no standards prescribed for a particular food article, a seller is free to add poison/insects/putrid substance to it or sell it by injuriously affecting its nature, substance or quality.

The only benefit which the accused can get in case of such proprietary food is that there cannot ordinarily be a violation of section 2(ia)(m) of PFA Act which pertains to violation of prescribed standards.

22. Similarly, there is no material to show that the food article in question contained any substance affecting injuriously the nature, substance or quality thereof, so as to bring it under the purview of section 2(ia)(b) of PFA Act.
There was no opinion given by the PA that the vegetable oil found in the burfi was injuriously affecting its nature, substance or quality.
The extent of such oil is not known.
It is not the case that some other ingredient of burfi was substituted with a cheaper vegetable oil.

Thus,
in the absence of any such evidence, it cannot be said that there is violation of section 2(ia)(b) of the PFA Act.

23. But as far as Section 2(ia)(a) of the PFA Act is concerned, the prosecution has to establish that the Khoya Burfi sold ("Sale" as per section 2(xiii) of PFA Act includes sale for analysis, offer for sale,
exposing for sale and attempt to sell) by the accused was not of the nature, substance or quality which it represented to be.

24. It is to be seen that when the Notice in Form-VI Ex. PW-1/B was prepared and given to the accused vendor, upon asking of the FI PW-1, he himself and in his own handwriting disclosed the ingredients of the food article being sold by him.
He informed that the Khoya Burfi had been prepared using Khoya, Sugar, Pista pieces and Badam pieces.
Apparently, he never disclosed presence of any vegetable oil in the food article.
Apparently, the ingredients were disclosed by the accused on asking of the FI and in his own handwriting.
This fact has never been denied by the accused.

It is not the case of the accused that such an ingredient had been disclosed by him or that he had forgotten to mention vegetable oil as an ingredient or that the FI did not write complete ingredients as disclosed by him or that he was forced or threatened or pressurized to write incomplete ingredients.
No such stand has been taken at any stage of trial nor any representation was made to the PFA Department between the date of lifting of the sample and filing of the complaint.

Therefore, if some vegetable oil is detected by the chemical expert which remains unexplained and which could not be attributed to the disclosed ingredients, then such presence of vegetable oil would be a violation of section 2(ia)(a) of the Act.
25. There is no merit in the argument of Ld. Counsel that a vendor is not required to disclose the ingredients of sweets in view of Rule 43(5) of PFA Rules.

This Rule deals with declarations that are required to be given in case of packed food in advertisements, price list, trade list, etc. in case of food article which contains an addition, admixture or deficiency which affects its purity.
This rule pertains to declarations on the food package which is a prepackaged food within the definitions given under the Act and Rules.
But when a food article is sold in loose condition, as in the present case, no such Rule would apply as packaging and labelling standards are not applicable to such food being sold loose.

Rule 43 falls in Part-VII of PFA Rules that deals with packaging and labelling Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs Pramod Kumar Jain on 19 September, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/80700135/
6 regulations.
Reliance on this Rule by the Ld.
Counsel in this manner is misfounded.
There is nothing to show that a vendor selling sweets can escape from disclosing correct ingredients or to conceal some ingredients of a food product (unless it is a trade secret).
Thus, no benefit can be derived by the accused on this count.

26. Similarly, the court does not find force in the stand of the Ld. Defence Counsel that there is no standard for 'extract fat' and therefore, no sample can be failed due to presence of the such fat.

It is correct that no standard has been prescribed for such extracted fat in food articles, but it is to be understood that the present case is not with respect to any deficiency or adulteration or sub-standardization in the extracted fat.
Rather the presence of fat in the form of vegetable oil in itself an issue here.
Irrespective of the quality of the extracted fat, the question here is how the fat was found in the food article when no such ingredient was disclosed by the vendor.
Here the court is not concerned if the extracted fat was of some other quality or nature.
The question is how the fat was found present when it was not declared as an ingredient.
This argument is without merit.

27. It is important to note here that the accused has not questioned the correctness of the PA report (though has disputed her opinion that the food article was adulterated) with respect to the presence of vegetable oil in the sample.
It is nowhere his case that no such vegetable oil was there in food article or that the vegetable oil had been wrongly detected or that some incorrect or unreliable method of analysis was used.
The only question to be determined is, if the vegetable oil as detected by the PA could be that of the pista and badam pieces which were added in the food article as an ingredient.
28. PA is a chemical expert whose report is admissible in evidence without formal proof under section 293 CrPC.
However, it does not mean that the report can be taken as a gospel truth and cannot be questioned on any ground.
As per section 293 CrPC, the accused has an option to apply and cross examine the PA.
Thus, such a report can always be questioned to seek any clarification or to seek explanation on any point on which the report is silent or doubtful.
But it is for the accused to avail this option available to him.
29. The PA is the best evidence to explain the things, having examined the sample and having given opinion on the basis of analytical values.

PA would be the best person to accept or deny the stand taken by the accused, who would explain the intricacies and validity of the tests performed and who would justify the reasons for the opinion given.

30. As far as the contents of the PA report Ex. PW-1/F is concerned, it is to be understood that the report given by the PA is only the final report arrived after detailed analysis and is in the prescribed format as provided under the PFA Rules.
It is not that this report is the complete and the only material available with the PA on the analysis.
All the other details with respect to the tests conducted, the analytical values, the calculations, etc. are recorded and maintained by the office of PA.
Such record can always be summoned from the office and can be proved and put to the PA during cross-examination.

7 31.

sentences.text: Therefore, if the accused wishes to ascertain the details of the testing methods which do not form part of final report Ex. PW-1/F, he is required to exercise his option under section 293 CrPC to apply and cross- examine the PA and also to call for the records from the PA office either during the cross-examination of PA or even in his defence evidence.
But if the accused fails to exercise this option, he cannot now choose to dispute the PA report on any point on which the report is silent.
He cannot now question the report on any remote hypothesis, assumptions or presumptions.
32. Instead of applying under section 293 CrPC to cross-examine the PA, the accused opted to examine DW-1A Sh. S. N. Mahendru, who happens to be a food chemical expert.

He had never analysed the sample in question but on the basis of his studies, knowledge and experience, deposed that the BR value of Almond Oil is 54-57 and that of Pista Oil is 61.5-66.5, that vegetable oil is covered under GMP (Good Manufacturing Practices) and can be used to prevent material from sticking to the container, and that Pista and Almond seeds have oil content.
33. As already stated, the accused has not exercised his option to apply under section 293 CrPC to cross-examine the PA.
She would have been the best person to explain the things, clarify the same and also to accept or rebut the stand of the accused.
In her absence, the court cannot simply assume that she would not have separated the Pista and Badam pieces from the sample commodity before subjecting it to chemical analysis.
It is quite possible that the analyst had removed or separated the pista and badam pieces.
But when no testimony of PA is there and no record from PA office has been called, the court cannot assume existence or absence of any such fact.

The court cannot, merely on the basis of assumptions and inferences, come to the conclusion that she would have definitely tested the Khoya Burfi with pista and badam pieces in it and would not have removed such pieces before subjecting the commodity to chemical analysis.
Therefore, it cannot be said with certainty that oil of Pista and Badam would definitely have come in the extracted fat and would have increased the BR value.
34. Even otherwise, the BR value detected by PA in this case is 49.5.
After going through the entire material on record, the court fails to find any basis on which this BR value could be explained by the accused.
Various products have different BR values.
BR value of ghee in Delhi is 40-43 and that of butter oil / milk fat (which is a part of khoa being milk product) is 40-44.
Various oils like coconut oil, cottonseed oil, groundnut oil, linseed oil, olive oil, sunflower oil, etc have various BR values.
Most of these items are standardized food articles and the rules prescribe the range under which their BR values can fall.

However, there is nothing on record to show as to what would be the BR value of Khoya and Sugar which were the primary disclosed ingredients of the khoya burfi, and up to what extent the BR value of such a khoa burfi would increase if pista and badam pieces are added to it in such quantity.
There is no evidence on record to show that the BR value of khoya burfi would go as high up to 49.5%.
If it was only a case of marginal increase, the court would still have assumed that the BR value increased due to addition of pista or badam pieces.
But the present is a case of substantial increase in BR value and not marginal increase.
35. As per DW-1A, the BR value of almond oil and pista oil is 54-57 and 61.5-66.5, respectively.
Therefore, it is clear that as far as BR value detected by the PA is concerned, the same is not only of pista oil and almond oil.

It follows that there was some vegetable oil the food article other than and Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs Pramod Kumar Jain on 19 September, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/80700135/
8 in addition to the pista and almond oils which might have come due to presence of pista and almond pieces.

sentences.text: And if the identity of the such added vegetable oil has not been disclosed by the accused, he cannot put the burden to this effect on the prosecution and claim that the PA should have identified such oil.
36. There is no merit in the stand of DW-1A that the analyst should have identified which other oil was present.
It is to be understood that not all vegetable oils are identifiable and it may be possible that some vegetable oil found in the article had not yet been identified.
It is possible that further tests were not conducted to identify the oils or that there were combination of two or more such oils making it impossible to detect the kinds of vegetable oils used.
But as far as PA is concerned, she was to go only by the declaration given by the accused in Form-VI.
If there was presence of some other oil otherwise not declared by the accused, then it was for the accused to explain and disclose the said oil.
As already said, the accused never opted to apply under section 293 CrPC and cross- examine the PA so as to question her on these aspects.
Similarly, the accused never sought to call for the record maintained by the PA which would have disclosed what tests were performed and might also have disclosed the identity of oils detected.

If the accused was having any doubt about the method used or the veracity of method or technical details of the same, he should have applied section 293 CrPC and cross examine her on all those points.
But when the accused has not exercised his option, he cannot question the PA report on the ground that it is silent on some aspects.
He cannot be allowed to get benefit of his own wrong and question the report on the basis of something on which it is silent.

Therefore, even if PA report is silent as to identification of vegetable oil so added by the accused, no infirmity can be attached to the PA report, as claimed by DW-1A.
37.

Ld. Defence Counsel while arguing the matter contended that the prosecution has not ruled out various possibilities of using contaminated utensils / implements, possibility of improper sampling,
possibility of the vegetable oil being added subsequently, possibility of the vegetable oil coming into the food product as GMP through the tray on which it was kept, possibility of the PA having added the BR value of pista and almond oil in giving his opinion etc.
38.
Well, the prosecution is required to prove its case beyond the shadow of reasonable doubt and not to prove the case beyond all remotest probabilities and possibilities.

Of course there are several defences available to the accused, but the prosecution is not required to rule out all the said remote possibilities and defences under the Sun which the accused might claim at the trial.

If any specific defence has been taken by the accused, it would be for the accused to establish the same by either pointing out the defects / infirmities in the prosecution case and / or by leading defence evidence.

But the accused cannot claim that all the remote possibilities have to be ruled out by the prosecution, irrespective of the fact that the such defences taken by the accused are contradictory and mutually destructive.
39. The record shows that the accused has been taking contradictory stands throughout the trial and his defence has never been consistent.

40. During the evidence of PW-1 and PW-2, the accused never took any stand to the effect that the vegetable oil had been used by him as lubricant as GMP, or that the oil detected by the PA was from Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs Pramod Kumar Jain on 19 September, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/80700135/
9 pista or badam pieces.

sentences.text: He never took stand that no vegetable oil was there in the food article as detected by the PA nor he questioned the PA report in any manner.

Rather during the evidence of these two witnesses, the accused took stand that the commodity in question had been mixed with hands and that the product in question belonged to 'Rameshwar' and not the accused.
41. Subsequently, his line of defence shifted to altogether different area.
During the cross-examination of PW-3, he never took the defences taken during cross-examination of PW-1 and PW-2.
He now did not claim that the product belonged to 'Rameshwar or that the product had been mixed with hands or that there had been some contamination in the utensils used.

Now he accepted the presence of vanaspati in the sample (thereby accepting the added vegetable oil in addition to badam and pista oil) by claiming that there was vanaspati on the spoon used by the FI to mix the commodity and on the sample bottles used by him in the proceedings.
Apparently, these defences were never taken by him during the evidence of PW-1 and PW-2 and no such suggestion was put to them.
In any case, no evidence has been led by the accused to this extent and such defences put to PW-3 have remained bald suggestions without any evidentiary proof.
No witness has been examined by the accused to fortify his stand that the spoon or bottles were having vanasapti which entered the food article in question.
This is as against the evidence of PW-1, PW-2 and PW-3 who categorically deposed on oath about the use of clean and dry knife, stainless steel spoon and sample glass bottles.
This is not a case where there is no evidence or doubtful evidence about use of clean and dry implements.
Rather there is positive evidence in the form of testimony of three PWs wherein they testified about use of clean and dry instruments / utensils / implements.

Ld. Defence Counsel has not been able to explain what other evidence he was expecting to establish this fact in addition to the corroborative evidence of three PWs as against mere bald suggestions put to them in cross-examination.
There is nothing to show that any contamination was there in the spoon or bottles in the manner suggested.

42. For that matter, once the accused has chosen to put such suggestions to the PWs, that vanaspati had entered the sample from spoon or bottles, he has virtually accepted that such vegetable oil was there in the sample addition to the pista and badam oil as claimed by him.

If his stand was that the vegetable oil detected by the PA was only from pista and badam pieces, there was no occasion for him to claim that vanaspati got added to the sample due to any contamination from the spoon or sample bottles.
43. Similarly, during cross-examination of PW-3, accused claimed that the oil can be put on the tray so as to avoid sticking the material to it.
Such a suggestion was denied by PW-3.
Apparently, no such stand was taken by the accused at any earlier stage of the trial particularly during the evidence of PW-1 and PW-2.

For that matter, even during the cross- examination of PW-3, the accused only sought his opinion as to if it would always be necessary to apply a layer of vegetable oil on the tray so as to make it non-sticky.
He never took any positive and certain stand to this effect at the trial or claimed or suggested to any PW that he had used vegetable oil on the tray as a lubricant.
It was only during his statement under section 313 CrPC that he for the first time categorically stated that his worker had applied vegetable oil on the tray.

But again, if he claims that the vegetable oil had been so used by him as a lubricant on the tray, there was no occasion for him to claim that the vegetable oil as detected by the PA was that of pista and badam pieces only.

Such stands are in contradiction Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs Pramod Kumar Jain on 19 September, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/80700135/
10 to each other.

sentences.text: 44. Even during his statement under section 313 CrPC, the accused took various contradictory stands.
He now did not claim that the sample commodity had been mixed with hands, as suggested by him to PW-1 and PW-2 during their cross-examination.
Similarly, he did not claim that the product in question had not been manufactured by him or that it belonged to Rameshwar, as suggested to PW-1 and PW-2.
Rather he took stand that "he" had put pista and badam pieces which contained vegetable oil.
By taking such stand, he has accepted that the food article had been manufactured by him only.
This further fortifies the stand of PW-2 who deposed that the accused had called Rameshwar who denied the supply of food article to him.

Once the accused has accepted that he had added the pista and badam pieces to the burfi, he has eventually accepted that the product had been manufactured by him only and not obtained from any third person.
At the same time, he took a contradictory stand and claimed that his worker had pasted some oil in the tray to avoid sticking burfi to the tray.
If he claimed that the product belonged to Rameshwar, then he would not have an occasion to say that his worker had used oild as lubricant.
There is no explanation for such contradictory and mutually destructive defences.
45. In any case, there is no evidence led by the accused to prove any of these defences.
No worker has been examined in defence who might have pasted vegetable oil on the tray as lubricant.
There is no witness who was present at the time of manufacturing of the commodity or who had seen any worker applying vegetable oil on the tray as a lubricant.
Therefore, there is no evidence in the form of testimony of any witness who could establish that the vegetable oil found by the PA in the sample was on account of such use of oil as a lubricant.
No name of any such worker has been disclosed by the accused so as to enable the court to summon and examine him.
46. Relying upon the evidence of PW-2, accused has claimed that the vegetable oil can be used as a lubricant under GMP.
True, vegetable oil can be used under GMP but the question is, if the accused ever took such a stand at the trial.
Apparently, not a single suggestion was put to any of the three PWs to the effect that the accused had used vegetable oil as a lubricant under GMP.
It was only when the evidence was over that the accused claimed in the statement for the first time by making positive statement that his worker had pasted some vegetable oil on the tray.

But other than this explanation given under section 313 CrPC, which obviously cannot be termed as 'evidence', there is no positive material on the basis of which the court may conclude that vegetable oil had been used in the present case as a lubricant which had entered into the food article so as to increase the BR value as opined by the PA to such an extent.
On the basis of material on record, it can be said that the stands taken by the accused are at huge variance and even contradictory, which have also remained not proved.
Therefore, such stands have to be rejected.
No other stand has been taken by the accused at the trial or during the arguments advanced.
47. It was upon the accused to show that the sample was having some vegetable oil which was a part of ingredients disclosed by him.
The burden was on the accused to show as to what was the identity of the vegetable oil as detected by the PA which was certainly not only the pista oil or badam oil.

If there was some other vegetable oil on account of some other addition which the accused did not disclose, then the offence would definitely be made out, irrespective of the fact if any harm was Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs Pramod Kumar Jain on 19 September, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/80700135/
11 caused to anyone or if the article injuriously affected the nature, quality or substance of the food commodity.

sentences.text: The accused has not disclosed and himself concealed the nature of vegetable oil which was there in the food article, which is certainly not pista oil and badam oil only, and even at the stage of trial, he has not disclosed all the ingredients of the food article which he was bound to disclose otherwise.
Therefore, he sold a food article which was not of the quality, nature or substance which he represented to be.

This would, therefore, be a violation of section 2(ia)(a) of PFA Act.
48.
In view of this discussion, it can be said that the complainant / prosecution has been able to establish its case and prove the guilt of the accused beyond the shadow of reasonable doubt.

It has been proved that the accused had stored / exposed for sale adulterated food in violation of section 2(ia)(a) of PFA Act, and has committed the offence punishable under section 7/16(1)(a) of PFA Act.
49.

Thus, the accused is held guilty and convicted for the offence punishable under section 16(1)(a)
of the PFA Act.
50.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
He is not facing trial for violation of section 2(ia)(m) of PFA Act.
12. Under section 2(ia)(a) of PFA Act, the prosecution has to establish that the purchaser had demanded a food article of a specific nature, substance or quality and the article sold was, to his prejudice, either not of the nature, substance or quality demanded, or was not of the nature,
substance or quality which it purported or represented to be.
Under section 2(ia)(b) of PFA Act, it has to be established that the food article contained any substance affecting injuriously the nature,
substance or quality thereof.
On the other hand, section 2(ia)(m) of PFA Act deals with situation where the quality or purity of an article falls below the prescribed standard or its constituents are present in quantities not within the prescribed limits of variability.
13. To begin with, it is an admitted position that the food article Khoya Burfi does not fall under any item of Appendix-B of the PFA Rules.
Proprietary Food, as per Rule 37-A of PFA Rules means a food which has not been standardised under the said Rules.
Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs Pramod Kumar Jain on 19 September, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/80700135/
4 18.
Once this fact is so established, section 27 of the General Clauses Act would come into play.
When a letter is sent through registered post at a correct and proper address, there would be a presumption of service under section 27 of the General Clauses Act in favour of the complainant.
The burden would not upon be the complainant to show delivery of the letter and such burden would now shift upon the accused to show that the letter was not so delivered despite having been sent at a correct address through registered post.
Thus, accused has failed to rebut the presumption under section 27 of the General Clauses Act.
Irrespective of time taken in investigating the matter and filing the complaint after obtaining sanction, it can be noted that no amount of delay could have produced vegetable oil in the food product if it was otherwise absent.
With such material in hand, it is clear that the food article "Pista Burfi" is not a standardised food article and thus, no standards have been prescribed under the PFA Rules which can be said to have been violated.
Even if a food article is not a standardised food article, it has to be free from adulteration and has to be pass the other tests upon being considered as a proprietary food.
It cannot be said that since there are no standards prescribed for a particular food article, a seller is free to add poison/insects/putrid substance to it or sell it by injuriously affecting its nature, substance or quality.
The only benefit which the accused can get in case of such proprietary food is that there cannot ordinarily be a violation of section 2(ia)(m) of PFA Act which pertains to violation of prescribed standards.
22. Similarly, there is no material to show that the food article in question contained any substance affecting injuriously the nature, substance or quality thereof, so as to bring it under the purview of section 2(ia)(b) of PFA Act.
There was no opinion given by the PA that the vegetable oil found in the burfi was injuriously affecting its nature, substance or quality.
The extent of such oil is not known.
It is not the case that some other ingredient of burfi was substituted with a cheaper vegetable oil.
Thus,
in the absence of any such evidence, it cannot be said that there is violation of section 2(ia)(b) of the PFA Act.
23. But as far as Section 2(ia)(a) of the PFA Act is concerned, the prosecution has to establish that the Khoya Burfi sold ("Sale" as per section 2(xiii) of PFA Act includes sale for analysis, offer for sale,
exposing for sale and attempt to sell) by the accused was not of the nature, substance or quality which it represented to be.
Therefore, if some vegetable oil is detected by the chemical expert which remains unexplained and which could not be attributed to the disclosed ingredients, then such presence of vegetable oil would be a violation of section 2(ia)(a) of the Act.
This rule pertains to declarations on the food package which is a prepackaged food within the definitions given under the Act and Rules.
But when a food article is sold in loose condition, as in the present case, no such Rule would apply as packaging and labelling standards are not applicable to such food being sold loose.
There is nothing to show that a vendor selling sweets can escape from disclosing correct ingredients or to conceal some ingredients of a food product (unless it is a trade secret).
Thus, no benefit can be derived by the accused on this count.
It is correct that no standard has been prescribed for such extracted fat in food articles, but it is to be understood that the present case is not with respect to any deficiency or adulteration or sub-standardization in the extracted fat.
Rather the presence of fat in the form of vegetable oil in itself an issue here.
It is nowhere his case that no such vegetable oil was there in food article or that the vegetable oil had been wrongly detected or that some incorrect or unreliable method of analysis was used.
28. PA is a chemical expert whose report is admissible in evidence without formal proof under section 293 CrPC.
However, it does not mean that the report can be taken as a gospel truth and cannot be questioned on any ground.
Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs Pramod Kumar Jain on 19 September, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/80700135/
7 31.
Therefore, if the accused wishes to ascertain the details of the testing methods which do not form part of final report Ex. PW-1/F, he is required to exercise his option under section 293 CrPC to apply and cross- examine the PA and also to call for the records from the PA office either during the cross-examination of PA or even in his defence evidence.
And if the identity of the such added vegetable oil has not been disclosed by the accused, he cannot put the burden to this effect on the prosecution and claim that the PA should have identified such oil.
It is to be understood that not all vegetable oils are identifiable and it may be possible that some vegetable oil found in the article had not yet been identified.
But as far as PA is concerned, she was to go only by the declaration given by the accused in Form-VI.
But when the accused has not exercised his option, he cannot question the PA report on the ground that it is silent on some aspects.
He cannot be allowed to get benefit of his own wrong and question the report on the basis of something on which it is silent.
Therefore, even if PA report is silent as to identification of vegetable oil so added by the accused, no infirmity can be attached to the PA report, as claimed by DW-1A.
37.
If any specific defence has been taken by the accused, it would be for the accused to establish the same by either pointing out the defects / infirmities in the prosecution case and / or by leading defence evidence.
But the accused cannot claim that all the remote possibilities have to be ruled out by the prosecution, irrespective of the fact that the such defences taken by the accused are contradictory and mutually destructive.
It has been proved that the accused had stored / exposed for sale adulterated food in violation of section 2(ia)(a) of PFA Act, and has committed the offence punishable under section 7/16(1)(a) of PFA Act.
49.
